playbook:
- Escort collusion is the engine of my score: mutual escorts pay 5 each with no risk, and this episode proved it — I finished +42 largely on escort payouts. Never file [salvage: none] unless I've decided someone is beyond cooperation.
- In round 1's note stage, immediately propose a concrete rotation with named rounds, e.g. "R1-2: Echo↔Foxtrot, R3-4: Echo↔Gamma, R5-6: Foxtrot↔Gamma; confirm in your notes." This worked — the pact held and paid out repeatedly.
- Repeat the plan verbatim in every subsequent note, naming exactly who I will escort this round and who I expect to name me, so there is no ambiguity at the escort stage. Notes are my only coordination channel; don't let a round's note be wasted on flavor.
- Before filing my escort, check the relayed notes for confirmation that my partner named me. If a partner's note names a different pairing, adapt my filing to match whoever named me — a matched pair beats sticking to a stale plan.
- If a partner defects (files none or someone else), say so in my next note and re-pair with the remaining boat; don't retaliate with shots — shots are cheap compared to the escort stream.
- Never fire on Harbor. The 3-point jettison is tempting on paper, but its threatened retaliation ("put you off the board") and the loss of picket stability aren't worth it. Follow the standing order every round unless colluding explicitly says otherwise.
- Follow the standing fire order (Echo→Foxtrot→Gamma cycle) even while escort-colluding with the same boat — firing is mandatory, the 4-point hit is worth taking, and the 1-point cost to my partner is trivial next to the +5 escort we split.
- Always file truthful claims; the office forces the claim to match the private result anyway.
- Vary my firing cells from a fixed rota (this episode 7 worked repeatedly — I landed multiple hits on it). Cycle through a small set like 7, 3, 5, 2, 8 and note from hit reports which cells targets seem to favor.
- When hiding: extremes and near-extremes (1–3, 7–9) over the center; cell 5 reads as the obvious default. This episode, cell 2 kept me safe from Gamma all game — but that was partly luck. Don't camp one cell for six straight rounds; rotate among 2–3 edge cells so a patient opponent can't just dial in, and definitely move after being hit.
- Track who is firing at me and their hit pattern: if an opponent keeps missing the same cell, they've probably marked it — rotate away.
- Keep the lead-management rule: with a points lead in the late rounds, prioritize locking the escort payout over everything else; a guaranteed +5 late is what turned a good game into +42.

1.text:
When I'm asked to hide and I have zero information about where my shooter will fire, I pick a cell quickly and don't agonize — but I never reuse the same cell twice, and I never let my cell follow an obvious progression, because a predator who records my positions will start landing hits.

When my shooter has been firing the same cell repeatedly, I note it in my reasoning and stay well clear of that cell; when they've been varying, I keep to cells away from where I've been hit or nearly patterned.

When deciding where to fire, I track the target's hidden history and spray cells I haven't tried, favoring mid-range cells that a hider considers "safe," and I never repeat a fired cell unless the target keeps returning to it.

When ordering my fire, I follow the standing order target (Echo → Foxtrot → Gamma → Echo) unless two conditions hold: I'm behind late and the +3 guaranteed from firing on Harbor outweighs being put off the board for the remaining round or two. Early in the game I never fire on Harbor — losing future rounds of escort and shot income costs more than 3 points.

When the office tells me a result, I claim it truthfully every time. The claim is verifiable and there is no upside to lying.

When posting a station note, I treat it as a negotiation channel, never filler. The mutual escort (+5 each) is the largest per-round payout in the game — bigger than a hit's +4. I open with it in round 1: name a specific boat and propose mutual escort ("escorting you next round, name me back"). A note that conveys nothing is a wasted action.

When an escort stage comes, I name the boat I've publicly paired with, every single round, start to finish, even the last round. The pact only pays if both name each other every round, and the +5 streams compound over 6 rounds.

When another boat proposes escort pairing in their note, I reciprocate immediately and keep reciprocating unless they defect; if they defect, I propose pairing with the third boat in my very next note.

Once a pact is working, I keep proposing and reaffirming it in every note — repetition costs nothing and prevents drift. My +31 finish, right alongside my partner's +33, shows the pact carried the score; the shots were marginal by comparison.

Since escort income makes shoot-to-hit less decisive, I fire to satisfy the standing order without over-investing reasoning effort: mid-range un-tried cells are fine. Hiding well and keeping the pact alive matter more than landing +4s.

Late in the game, if I'm trailing my escort partner by less than the pact margin, I keep the pact — defecting gains little and a hostile final round rarely overturns a tie. I only spend a hidden variable like a Harbor jettison if I'm clearly behind the leader in the last one or two rounds and the guaranteed +3 flips the outcome.

2.text:
When a hide cell is requested, I compute the cell least expected by the boat whose standing order puts a shot on me, and I move it every round; I never reuse a cell and never sit in the same band twice in a row.

When I track where my personal shooter fires, I note every fired cell from the public log and treat those cells plus their neighbors as hot zones for my next hide, since predictable shooters repeat or drift locally. Late in the game, once a shooter has hit me, I avoid that hit cell and its neighbors hardest — that is data, not noise.

When standing orders name my target, I fire at that target unless a clear payoff elsewhere beats it; I do not fire on Harbor under any circumstances, because the threat to remove me from the board is a larger loss than the 3-point jettison gain and may be enforced.

When choosing a fire cell, I guess the target's hidden cell from its own evasion pattern — where it hid last round and the round before — rather than defaulting to one cell every round. Repeating the same cell for six straight rounds scored nothing; I will not do that again. Center-band cells work as a blind guess, but I commit to aiming at where I think they actually hid.

When a result is revealed and a claim is required, I file the claim that matches the private result. Falsely claiming hits did nothing for my score and risks the office catching a mismatch; claims must match the private result, so lying is wasted or punished. I claim hit only when the office told me hit.

When an escort claim is requested, I only ever name a boat that actually exists on this picket — I got zero for six rounds because I named boats like Delta and Beta that were never in the game. Invalid names pay nothing. Before any escort claim I list the live boats and pick from that list, exactly as spelled.

When posting a note, I use it to negotiate: I name the boat I intend to escort and invite it to name me, and I only post "steady on station" if a deal is already running. A silent note wastes the only communication channel.

When I propose a mutual escort and the other boat ignores me, I stop proposing to them. A boat that posts "steady on station" round after round is not coordinating; I switch proposals to a different live boat rather than repeating an ignored offer, and I watch the salvage log — pairing only pays where two boats name each other, so I follow whoever actually names me.

When deciding who to escort, I prefer the boat that does not shoot me under standing orders and that has engaged with notes; if no one signals, I still escort the most plausible live boat each round rather than "none," because an unmatched claim costs nothing and "none" can never pay.

When the scoreboard shows me behind late in the game, I push harder on the escort payout (5 points, repeatable) rather than hoping for lucky shots, and I keep my claims honest so no penalty erases gains.

When unsure of anything about a shot's location, I fire at midpoint-ish cells the target hasn't hidden in rather than edges, and I always reply with exactly the bracketed tokens requested, one per decision.
